clue.text: As long as you've got flies buzzing, sleep goes west

indicators.note: insects that are buzzing dart about wildly, so these letters fly into a new order
in an across clue, heading west means running right to left, backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging
a nap is a short sleep

explanation.surface: A gloomy observation that wherever there are flies, nobody gets any rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flies' reads as a noun, the insects, but it is just letters to be reshuffled. The definition is a whole phrase: how long you've got is your LIFESPAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifespan is the length of time a person lives, so it measures the period one has been given.

clue.text: Final requirement of shoemakers

blocks.note: first meaning: coming at the end
second meaning: the foot-shaped block a cobbler builds a shoe around

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as the last thing a cobbler needs, but 'Final' is one meaning and the cobbler's tool is the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means coming at the end, and is also the wooden or metal foot model used in shoemaking.

clue.text: Plant initially lost in transmission

indicators.note: what happens initially comes at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: a fax is a document sent down a phone line
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A plant that somehow went missing while being shipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost in transmission' sounds like a phrase about garbled messages; it is really one letter placed inside a fax.
explanation.definitionFit: Flax is a blue-flowered crop plant grown for linen fibre and linseed oil.

clue.text: Cringe as guv'nor loses last mark

indicators.note: losing the last of something means its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a squire, the local landowner and boss, minus his final letter
M is the abbreviation for mark, as in the old German currency

explanation.surface: Someone flinches as the boss drops a grade from their assessment.
explanation.walkthrough: Guv'nor is a colloquial British word for a boss or master, which a squire was in his village.
explanation.definitionFit: To squirm is to wriggle with embarrassment or discomfort, much as one cringes.

clue.text: Associates Bill with curious topless capers

indicators.note: without a top, the word loses its head, its opening letter

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
quaint means oddly old-fashioned
dances (lively capers) without the first letter

explanation.surface: Bill's friends get up to odd semi-naked antics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is an account, and 'capers' are leaps or dances here, not pickled buds.
explanation.definitionFit: Acquaintances are people one knows slightly, so they are associates rather than close friends.

clue.text: Judge with leer grabbing tip of girl's elbow

indicators.note: to grab something is to hold it within one's grasp
only the tip, the leading letter, is wanted from the next word

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for judge
to ogle is to leer at
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lecherous judge leers and grabs a girl by the elbow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elbow' looks like a body part at the end of the scene, but it is a verb: to nudge or jostle.
explanation.definitionFit: To joggle is to jolt or shake slightly, as one does when nudging someone with an elbow.

clue.text: Solid nuts with odd filling? Refiners use them

indicators.note: going nuts means going crazy, so the letters are thrown into disorder
a filling sits inside something, like jam in a sponge

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging
rum is an old British word for strange or odd

explanation.surface: A snack question: solid nuts with a peculiar centre, of the sort refiners might use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filling' is the container signal here, with the odd word placed inside the rearranged letters. 'Solid nuts' reads like food, but 'nuts' is the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil refineries store and ship crude and refined products in large metal barrels, which are oil drums.

clue.text: Drunkard first to give up eco-unfriendly car

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, backwards
this places the following piece at the front of the word

blocks.note: to sag is to give way under weight
a guzzler drinks greedily

explanation.surface: A drunk driver should be the first to give up a car that burns fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give up' reads as quit, but 'give' means sag and 'up' turns it over. Gas is the American word for petrol.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas guzzler is a car with heavy fuel consumption, and so harmful emissions, hence bad for the environment.

clue.text: Heartbroken, fated never to reach the stars?

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters can be reassembled differently

blocks.note: the first five letters are taken as written, before rearranging
bound to happen means fated to

explanation.surface: A heartbroken dreamer laments being destined never to achieve greatness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartbroken' seems one word of feeling, but it splits into a word and its anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something earthbound is tied to the ground and cannot fly upwards, so it will never get to space.

clue.text: Band's current position

blocks.note: first meaning: a long-running British rock group
second meaning: the existing state of affairs

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a group's place in the charts; the 's stands for 'is', joining a rock band to a Latin phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase names the existing state of things, and also a famous British rock group of the 1970s onwards.

clue.text: Grandfather has time here, apparently

blocks.note: first meaning, playful: a grandfather clock shows the hours on its dial
second meaning: judging by appearances

explanation.walkthrough: The grandfather is a grandfather clock, a tall pendulum clock, not an old man with spare time.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means judging by how things look at first, which is what 'apparently' says.

clue.text: Genuine reflection capturing sun beam

indicators.note: a mirror reflection shows things back to front
to capture is to take and hold inside

blocks.note: real means genuine
S is the abbreviation for sun, as in Sunday

explanation.surface: A true image of sunlight caught and reflected as a ray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun beam' looks like one word split, but 'sun' is a letter and 'beam' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser is an intense, narrow ray of light, a beam in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Kick over milestone

blocks.note: to kick a habit is to break it
finished, as in 'it's all over' or 'we're through'

explanation.surface: Someone boots a roadside marker stone over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kick over' looks like one verb, to topple; read separately it is quit plus finished.
explanation.definitionFit: A breakthrough is a significant advance or discovery, a landmark achievement in a process.

clue.text: Sussex headline from 1066 not right? It's disputed

indicators.note: 'not' says a letter is absent, so it is taken away

blocks.note: a newspaper headline after the Norman invasion at Hastings, in Sussex
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Imagining the 1066 news in Sussex, with a hint that it might be wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Sussex is the southern English county where William of Normandy landed in 1066; a headline might read 'Normans land'.
explanation.definitionFit: No man's land is unoccupied ground between opposing forces, territory claimed or fought over.

clue.text: Fitted partitions holding up books

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, backwards
to hold is to keep something between them

blocks.note: two walls, plural partitions
OT is the Old Testament, the books of the Bible's first part

explanation.surface: Built-in shelving between dividing walls, propping up books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding up books' paints shelves, but 'up' turns the books round and 'holding' puts them between the walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Wall-to-wall describes a carpet laid across a whole floor, the fitted kind that covers it entirely.

clue.text: Yes, yes, yes!

blocks.note: OK is an informal yes
ay is an old or dialect yes, as in 'the ayes have it'

explanation.walkthrough: The repetition looks like enthusiasm, but each yes does its own job: one defines, the other two build the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Okay is an informal expression of agreement or assent, used just like that affirmative reply.

clue.text: Piece of music theory oddly accepted by popular singer

indicators.note: taken oddly, only the letters in odd-numbered places are kept
something accepted is taken in, so it goes inside

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
first, third and fifth letters
a mezzo-soprano, a female singer

explanation.surface: A pop star warmly receives some oddball musical theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular singer' reads as a pop star, but splits into two parts with the theory letters slotted between them.
explanation.definitionFit: An intermezzo is a short movement or interlude played between larger sections of an opera or other work.

clue.text: Prized horse carrying me after end of battle

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
to carry something is to hold it within
this puts the first piece behind the one named next

blocks.note: last letter of the word
a steed is a horse
taken as written

explanation.surface: A valued warhorse carries the rider home after the fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prized horse' reads as one phrase about a champion animal; the definition is just the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Esteemed means highly regarded or valued, as is anything treasured and respected.

clue.text: This rating would make "A" seem banal

indicators.note: making one thing out of another implies reworking the same materials

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: A complaint that some grade or score would make a top mark look dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' sounds like a score, and 'A' like a top grade, but a rating is a naval rank below officer.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Royal Navy, ratings are non-commissioned sailors, and an able seaman is one such grade.

clue.text: Sound of empty vessel

indicators.note: what something sounds like is how it is heard when spoken

blocks.note: vain means empty, as in futile or hollow

explanation.surface: The proverbial hollow noise made by an empty container.
explanation.walkthrough: It echoes the proverb 'empty vessels make the most noise', but the vessel is one carrying blood.
explanation.definitionFit: A vein is a blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart.

clue.text: Insult current panel

blocks.note: in means current or fashionable
a jury is a panel of judges or jurors

explanation.walkthrough: 'Insult' looks like a verb, but it is a noun in its medical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors use insult to mean physical harm or damage to the body, which is an injury.

clue.text: Diversionary tactics from Havana?

blocks.note: the surface reading: ploys to distract attention
the setter's reading: a Havana is a Cuban cigar, which puffs out clouds that hide things

explanation.walkthrough: Havana suggests Cuban political tricks, but a Havana is also a cigar, which literally produces a haze.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, these are ruses to hide one's real intentions; literally, clouds of vapour used to conceal.

clue.text: Sanctimonious politician, an unpleasant type

blocks.note: pi is British slang short for pious
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A holier-than-thou politician, dismissed as a nasty character.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a vague insult for the definition; it is a specific one.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimp lives off the earnings of prostitutes, a thoroughly disreputable sort of person.

clue.text: Kiss included in wartime offensive message

indicators.note: something included in another is placed within it

blocks.note: the Tet Offensive of 1968 in the Vietnam War
X is the symbol for a kiss

explanation.surface: A love note slipped into an aggressive military dispatch.
explanation.walkthrough: Tet is the Vietnamese New Year, and the offensive named after it is the one the setter means.
explanation.definitionFit: A text is a short written communication sent by phone, a message in modern usage.

clue.text: Alert, in marine style?

blocks.note: à la, the French phrase, means in the manner of
RM is the Royal Marines
completes the phrase 'in ... style', which is what à la means

explanation.surface: Being on guard the way a soldier at sea is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In marine style' reads 'à la RM', the way a Royal Marine does it; 'style' just completes that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm is a warning signal, the same thing as an alert, both nouns.

clue.text: Vesuvius very loud in eruption, but not very penetrating

indicators.note: an erupting volcano throws everything about, so the letters land in a new order
'but not' sets something aside, removing it from the rest

blocks.note: the volcano near Naples, taken as written
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A volcano blasting away loudly, yet its lava does not seep far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not very penetrating' looks like the definition; only 'penetrating' is, with 'not very' removing one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffusive describes something that spreads through and permeates, so it is pervading or seeping in.

clue.text: Meal regularly eaten by Dandy kid

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is taken
something eaten is swallowed up inside

blocks.note: a dude is a dandy, a fop
second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A child eating dinner on schedule out of the Dandy comic.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dandy was a long-running British children's comic; 'kid' looks like a child, but it is a verb, to fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To kid someone is to tease or fool them, so it is to trick or mislead them.

clue.text: Corset originally pulled up tight doesn't slip

indicators.note: the original part of a word is its beginning, so first letters are kept

blocks.note: stays is an old word for a boned corset
first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A corset laced up firmly will not slide down.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene is about underwear that holds; 'stays' is the historic name for the very garment.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay put is to remain in place without moving, so the item does not shift or slide.
